title: Micro-checkpoint KV protocol + GPU occupancy watermarking for graceful OOM recovery
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Summary:
This ticket defines and implements a combined run-time protocol to avoid and recover from GPU OOMs during continuous batching by: (1) writing lightweight, per-request micro-checkpoints of critical KV state, and (2) maintaining a GPU occupancy watermark that signals progressive degradation actions (token shaping, quantized shadow-model fallback, and speculative replay). The goal is to enable fast, deterministic recovery for mid-request OOMs and to gracefully degrade latency/quality with observable SLO tradeoffs rather than hard failures.

Motivation and context:
We still see rare but customer-visible tail OOMs when large concurrent steady-state batches interact with long-context requests. Current eviction-only approaches can lead to request aborts or full model fallback with poor latency/quality characteristics. Micro-checkpointing plus an occupancy watermark gives a graduated, transactional way to reduce live working set and recover in-flight requests without full restart. This complements existing eviction and model-fallback systems (see ENG-215001).

High-level approach:
1) Micro-checkpoints: for each request that causes or touches large KV segments (long-context or prefix-heavy), write a tiny immutable checkpoint entry containing: request id, minimal KV delta summary (references to segments and small fingerprint), and a compact replay plan. Checkpoints are kept in GPU-resident ring buffers when possible; they can be spilled to host as compressed delta if occupancy passes a threshold.
2) Occupancy watermark: the runtime maintains two watermarks: SAFE (normal), STRESS (begin degradation), and CRITICAL (trigger immediate micro-fallback). Watermark is computed from real-time GPU alloc/peak windows, batch admission queue length, and active KV footprint percent.
3) Progressive degradation ladder: on STRESS, runtime begins token-budget shaping for new requests (soft max tokens, early compression for KV reads); on CRITICAL, runtime uses micro-checkpoints to rollback or replay minimal KV segments and enacts shadow-model fallbacks (quantized 4-bit micro-models or shorter-sequence variants) for affected in-flight requests.
4) Speculative replay: when micro-checkpoint indicates a recoverable in-flight state, runtime can replay a reduced token sequence into a shadow model instance to complete the user response without rehydrating the full original KV in GPU memory. This avoids full eviction + model reload cycles.

Why unique / expected benefits:
- Reduce hard failures by converting them to fast, deterministic recoveries or quality-degraded responses.
- Lower tail latency from OOM-induced restarts.
- Preserve high-throughput steady-state behavior; micro-checkpoints are tiny and usually stay resident with low overhead.

Non-goals:
- Not a replacement for long-term KV eviction policy improvements (we still need smarter eviction windows).
- Not intended to support arbitrary-sized snapshots; micro-checkpoints must be compact by design.
acceptance_criteria: End-to-end canary demonstrating no hard OOMs for synthetic workload with long-context mix (50k seq tokens across concurrent requests) at 95th percentile load
Micro-checkpoint write+restore latency < 2ms on GPU-resident ring buffer path; < 10ms on host-spill path
Occupancy watermark correctly transitions SAFE->STRESS->CRITICAL in controlled stress test and triggers degradation ladder actions
Shadow-model fallback produces coherent responses for at least 80% of degraded requests in canary; quality regression tracked and linked
Instrumentation + dashboard showing metric parity: OOM count down, tail latency improvement, and percent of requests recovered via checkpoint vs full restart
Automated chaos test that simulates preemption and verifies speculative replay recovers 90% of affected in-flight requests
implementation_notes: Work split across runtime (C++), admission controller, and model-serving planner. Runtime must expose lightweight checkpoint API: create_checkpoint(request_id, fingerprint, segment_refs, replay_plan) and restore_checkpoint(id, target_model). Ring buffer allocator handles GPU path; fallback compressor for host spill. Admission controller uses watermark thresholds and publishes events to tracing. Model planner needs ability to select quantized shadow model variants and coordinate speculative replay. Expect ~3 PRs: runtime core, planner change, and console instrumentation integration (dashboard).
testing_plan: 1) Unit tests for checkpoint serialization and small-spill compressor. 2) Integration canary in staging: synthetic workload generator (long-prefix + varied batch sizes). 3) Chaos job that kills/evicts segments mid-request and validates recovery path. 4) A/B: enable on 10% of low-risk shard pool for 48h, compare tail OOMs and latency. 5) Post-rollout: monitor quality regression alerts tied to prompt-evals (see Optimize hooks).
risks_and_mitigation: Checkpoint bloat: restrict checkpoint size and enforce compaction; monitor checkpoint rate and auto-throttle writes
Replay correctness: start with conservative replay plans (only stateless prefix salvage) and expand after validation
Performance regression: benchmark micro-checkpoint hot path; add runtime flag to disable zero-cost hot-path writes if regression detected
Complexity of shadow models: pin to curated small-quantized variants in the model catalog; require gating and canary before broader use
rollout_plan: Phase 1: Feature flag gated implementation in staging + synthetic canary. Phase 2: Canary on 5% of runtime shards with telemetry only. Phase 3: 25% rollout with automatic rollback on OOM or latency regression thresholds. Phase 4: global rollout if canary metrics stable for 72h.
